studies.title: Potassium supplementation lowers blood pressure and increases urinary kallikrein in essential hypertensives.
studies.abstract: In order to eludicate possible mechanism(s) involved in the blood pressure reduction induced by potassium (K) supplementation, we studied the changes of BP and of some of its regulatory systems, including levels of urinary kallikrein (UKal)--an index of renal kallikrein production. Twenty-four untreated essential hypertensives, with a basal BP of 147/96 +/- 13/7 mmHg and normal renal function, received in crossover, double-blind, randomised fashion, 64 mmol KCl or placebo during two periods of 4 weeks each. At the 4th week of potassium supplementation systolic, diastolic and mean BPs decreased by 6.3 +/- 2 (P less than 0.01), 3.0 +/- 2 and 4.1 +/- 2 (P less than 0.05) mmHg respectively for the supine position, and 5.0 +/- 2, 4.0 +/- 2 (P less than 0.05) and 4.0 +/- 1 (P less than 0.05) mmHg for the standing position. Urinary potassium (K) increased from 55 +/- 4 to 123 +/- 6 mmol/24 hours (P less than 0.001) and UKal from 692 +/- 69 to 1052 +/- 141 mU/24 hours (P less than 0.01). Serum K rose from 3.8 +/- 0.1 mEq/l to 4.1 +/- 0.1 mmol/l (P less than 0.001) and PRA from 0.77 +/- 0.12 to 0.99 +/- 0.14 ng/ml/h (P less than 0.05). Correlations were observed between UKal and urinary K (r = 0.44, P less than 0.0001); between differences in UKal and urinary K and in UKal and urinary Na (r = 0.50, P less than 0.0005 and r = 0.48, P less than 0.001 respectively).(ABSTRACT TRUNCATED AT 250 WORDS)

studies.title: Clinical trial of gossypol as a male contraceptive drug. Part II. Hypokalemia study.
studies.abstract: A randomized controlled study was designed to evaluate the merit of whether ingesting potassium salt or potassium (K) blocking agent while using gossypol contraceptive drug could alleviate the symptom of hypokalemia. Results indicate that K salt supplementation did not reverse the gossypol-related hypokalemia and that the blocking agent triamterene did not prevent loss of or enhance the retention of serum K. A randomized, controlled study was designed to determine whether ingestion of potassium salt or a potassium blocking agent in conjunction with use of the male contraceptive gossypol could alleviate the symptom of hypokalemia noted in an earlier study. The 120 male volunteers were randomly assigned to 1 of 4 groups: gossypol 20 mg/day, gossypol 20 mg/day with potassium chloride 1.5 gm, gossypol 20 mg/day with triamterene 50 mg, and a control group. No pregnancies occurred among the wives of volunteers in the 3 gossypol-treated groups during the 12-month study period. A general trend of declining blood pressure by the end of the treatment period was noted in the 3 gossypol-treated groups. The serum potassium decline persisted until the end of the 1st treatment year for the 3 study groups but not for controls. Gossypol itself produced the least decline in serum potassium, followed by the gossypol-potassium chloride group and finally by the gossypol-triamterene regimen. This may be an indication that gossypol alone causes renal impairment, and therefore potassium supplementation and a blocking agent may have no effect on the restoration of potassium to normal levels.

studies.title: Hyperkalemia risk and potassium trajectory after finerenone initiation: a real-world cohort study.
studies.abstract:
Background

Finerenone improves cardiovascular and kidney outcomes in patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease; however, hyperkalemia remains a safety concern in routine practice. We evaluated the incidence of hyperkalemia, factors associated with its occurrence, and temporal patterns of serum potassium after finerenone initiation.

Methods

We conducted a single-center retrospective observational cohort study of patients who initiated finerenone between May 2022 and August 2025. The primary outcome was incident hyperkalemia (serum potassium ≥ 5.5 mEq/L). Candidate variables were selected using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO)-penalized Cox regression, and associations were estimated using multivariable Cox proportional hazards models. Potassium trajectories were assessed using mixed-effects models over 12 months (6 months before and after finerenone initiation), with subgroup analyses by kidney function and baseline potassium.

Results

Among 289 eligible patients, 280 were included (mean age 68 years; 68% male; mean baseline eGFR of 36.8 mL/min/1.73 m2). Hyperkalemia occurred in 38 patients. Incident hyperkalemia was associated with higher baseline potassium and log-transformed C-reactive protein and with use of diuretics and potassium binders. Mean serum potassium increased by approximately 0.10 mEq/L over six months, with the largest rise in the first 1-2 months. Patients with eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 or baseline potassium ≥ 4.5 mEq/L had higher potassium levels throughout follow-up.

Conclusions

Finerenone was generally well tolerated, with modest potassium increases. In our real-world cohort, hyperkalemia occurred in a notable proportion of patients, underscoring the importance of early monitoring, particularly in those with reduced kidney function or elevated baseline potassium.

studies.title: Supplementation of calcium, magnesium, phosphate, and potassium in critically ill patients: A multicenter cohort study.
studies.abstract:
Objective

To investigate hospital-level variation in the supplementation of calcium, magnesium, phosphate, and potassium in critically ill patients.

Design

Retrospective cohort study.

Setting

Premier Healthcare Database of inpatients from the USA.

Patients

Adults (age ≥ 18 years) admitted to an intensive care unit (ICU) on hospital day 1 between October 1, 2022 and July 31, 2024, who had at least one calcium (total or ionized), magnesium, phosphate, or potassium level measured in an ICU between day 2 and 28. We excluded patients with renal failure, a pregnancy-related diagnosis, and intracranial bleeding on admission.

Interventions

Calcium, magnesium, phosphate, or potassium supplementation.

Measurements and main results

We included 47,988 patients from 67 ICUs across 52 hospitals, totaling 167,621 patient-days with a measurement of one of the studied electrolytes. Median age was 64 years (interquartile range [IQR] 52-74) and 46% (22,057) were female. There were 38,621 patients (80.5%) with a minimum value below a lower limit of normal, and 33,626 (70.1%) patients who received supplementation. Across hospitals, the median (IQR) percentages receiving supplementation per day were: calcium 9.4% (6.7-12.2); magnesium 28.6% (22.6-35.0); phosphate 19.1% (15.9-23.2); potassium 28.9% (25.8-34.6). From a multilevel model, the median relative odds of supplementation, comparing any two hospitals, ranged from 1.51 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.48-1.55) for potassium to 2.09 (95% CI 1.99-2.19) for magnesium. At most hospitals, there were no calcium or phosphate levels at which the percentage receiving supplementation exceeded 50%. At 75% of hospitals there was a magnesium level at which the percentage receiving magnesium supplementation was 50% or more (range: 1.5-2.1 mg/dL), and at 96% of hospitals there was an analogous potassium level (range: 3.3-3.9 mmol/L).

Conclusion

Supplementation of calcium, magnesium, phosphate, or potassium is common in critically ill patients and varies across hospitals, suggesting a need for randomized trials to clarify optimal supplementation practices.

studies.title: Characterizing the impact of magnesium and potassium-supplemented hydration with cisplatin and the subsequent electrolyte replacement requirements.
studies.abstract: Cisplatin-associated electrolyte dysregulation is a prevalent therapy-related adverse effect. There are numerous electrolyte-supplemented hydration regimens that have been evaluated, however these studies focused on the development of nephrotoxicity. The objective of this study was to characterize the impact of magnesium and potassium-supplemented hydration during cisplatin administration on subsequent magnesium and potassium imbalances. A single-region retrospective study from central Texas at Baylor Scott & White Cancer Clinics who were treated with two or more cycles of cisplatin were included. Standard hydration for this study was defined as normal saline before and after cisplatin along with potassium chloride 10 mEq and magnesium sulfate 1 g added to the cisplatin bag. A total of 477 patients were included in the study with376 patients receiving the standard hydration. Overall, 17 percent of patients experienced a potassium level below 3.5 mEq/L, but no major depletion was observed. Thirty-three percent of the patients experienced a magnesium level below 1.8 mg/dL, and time to first rescue magnesium supplementation was 4 weeks. Our study demonstrated despite routine magnesium and potassium supplementation in hydration, magnesium imbalances were observed. Potassium levels post cisplatin administration were maintained with minimal routine supplementation in hydration.

studies.title: Gitelman syndrome.
studies.abstract: Hypokalaemia is a common clinical disorder, the cause of which can usually be determined by the patient's clinical history. Gitelman syndrome is an inherited tubulopathy that must be considered in some settings of hypokalaemia. We present the case of a 60-year-old male patient referred to our nephrology department for persistent hypokalaemia. Clinical history was positive for symptoms of orthostatic hypotension and polyuria. There was no history of drugs consumption other than potassium supplements. Complementary evaluation revealed hypokalaemia (2.15 mmol/l), hypomagnesaemia (0.29 mmol/l), metabolic alkalosis (pH 7.535, bicarbonate 34.1 mmol/l), hypereninaemia (281.7 U/ml), increased chloride (160 mmol/l) and sodium (126 mmol/l) urinary excretion and reduced urinary calcium excretion (0.73 mmol/l). Renal function, remainder serum and urinary ionogram, and renal ultrasound were normal. A diagnosis of Gitelman syndrome was established. We reinforced oral supplementation with potassium chloride and magnesium sulfate. Serum potassium stabilised around 3 mmol/l. The aim of our article is to remind Gitelman syndrome in the differential diagnosis of persistent hypokalaemia.

studies.title: Sex-Specific Cardiovascular Risk of Lower Potassium Intake in Patients with CKD.
studies.abstract:
Background

Lower potassium intake is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) in the general population, with observed sex differences. However, few studies have investigated the relationship between potassium intake and CVD in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), and sex-specific differences have not been well examined.

Methods

A total of 4,314 patients aged 18 years or older in Japan were prospectively followed for 5 years using data from the Fukuoka Kidney disease Registry study. The patients were divided into sex-specific quartiles according to the estimated potassium intake, which was calculated using the Tanaka formula from spot urine samples. The primary outcome was the occurrence of CVD events. Cox proportional hazards models were used to evaluate the association between the estimated potassium intake and CVD in the overall cohort with stratification by sex.

Results

Over a 5-year follow-up, 431 patients developed CVD (292 [12.1%] men and 139 [7.3%] women). In the overall cohort, patients in the lowest quartile of estimated potassium intake tended to have a higher hazard ratio (HR) for CVD than those in the highest quartile (HR [95% CI], 1.41 [0.97-2.03]). A significant interaction between sex and potassium intake was observed (p<0.001). In sex-stratified analyses, lower potassium intake was significantly associated with an increased risk of CVD in women (HR [95% CI]: men, 0.98 [0.63-1.53]; women, 2.97 [1.44-6.10]).

Conclusions

Lower estimated potassium intake is associated with a higher risk of CVD in patients with CKD, with a particularly strong association in women.

studies.title: Effect of oral potassium supplementation on urinary potassium excretion and its diagnostic value for primary aldosteronism.
studies.abstract: We aimed to: (1) explore the effect of oral potassium supplementation on urinary potassium excretion, and (2) evaluate the value of urinary potassium-related indicators in distinguishing primary aldosteronism (PA) from non-PA patients. A prospective study of 20 patients with hypertension and hypokalemia caused by renal potassium loss between November 2023 and April 2024 was conducted. Demographic features, 24-hour urine collection before and after potassium supplementation were all collected. The patients had a mean age of 49.38 years and 70% were male. Following a median potassium supplement dose of 8.50 g, serum potassium increased from 3.25 to 3.90 mmol/L ( Urinary potassium does not increase proportionally with serum potassium levels or the oral potassium dose, showing individual variability. Post-supplementation urinary potassium has greater diagnostic value for distinguishing PA than pre-supplementation indicators.

studies.title: Potassium additives in ultra-processed foods identified from food label-analysis: More than meets the eye.
studies.abstract:
Background and aim

Nutritional guidelines for managing hyperkalaemia in individuals with chronic kidney disease (CKD) emphasise an individualised approach, focusing on adjusting dietary potassium intake by selecting low-potassium foods and avoiding ultra-processed food (UPF). However, little is known about potassium additives in UPFs. Therefore, this study aimed to assess i) the prevalence of UPFs containing potassium additives across three supermarket chain stores, ii) which food categories most frequently contained potassium additives, iii) which potassium additives were most common and iv) which functional class were most common among potassium additives.

Methods

A cross-sectional label-analysis was conducted from September 2024 to December 2025. UPFs were identified according to the NOVA classification system. Three supermarket chain stores in Denmark were selected to capture a representative range of products. Products were examined via the supermarkets' online platforms and assigned to twelve predefined food categories, and the potassium additives they contained.

Results

After analysing 5884 UPFs, 27.8% of the products contained at least one potassium-based additive, while the presence of potassium additives was unknown for 6.5% of the products. Across all categories, products containing at least one potassium additive were most frequently observed in non-alcoholic beverages (70.9%), sauces (57.0%), fish, seafood and derivatives (44.5%), fruit, vegetables and derivatives (30.1%) and ready-to-eat products (29.6%). The most frequent potassium additive was E202 (potassium sorbate, 60.6%) followed by E950 (Acesulfame K, 19.7%) and E501 (Potassium carbonates, 8.8%).

Conclusion

Potassium additives are widespread in UPFs and can be a hidden source of potassium, particularly in non-alcoholic beverages, sauces, and fish, seafood and derivatives. These findings underline the importance of dietary guidance for individuals with CKD at risk of hyperkalaemia and raise awareness of additive exposure in food choices.

studies.title: Roles of WNK1 and mTORC2 in aldosterone-independent regulation of potassium secretion in the distal nephron.
studies.abstract:
Introduction

Precise regulation of kidney potassium excretion is essential for maintaining plasma potassium concentration within narrow limits in the face of wide variations in intake. Aldosterone has long been considered the key regulator of tubule potassium secretion. However, increasing evidence suggests that it plays a relatively limited role over a wide range of potassium ingestion. Here we investigated the roles of WNK1 kinase and the mTORC2 regulatory complex in potassium secretion in the distal nephron of mice.

Methods

We generated knockout (KO) mice where alternatively mTORC2 or the potassium-sensitive kinase, WNK1, were selectively disrupted in the late distal convoluted tubule and early connecting tubule (DCT2/CNTe), an important site of potassium secretion. KO mice were subjected to an acute increase in dietary potassium, after which fluid and electrolyte parameters were measured, and subcellular localization and activity of key ion channels were assessed using immunofluorescence and patch clamp, respectively. Phosphorylation state of mTORC2 targets was determined using Western blot.

Results

In mice lacking mTORC2 in the DCT2/CNTe, urinary potassium excretion failed to increase adequately in response to high potassium intake, while sodium, chloride and net urine output were excessive, resulting in hyperkalemia and fluid volume wasting. Immunofluorescence and patch clamp revealed that active apical membrane sodium channels (αENaC) in DCT2/CNe failed to increase. Furthermore, KO mice lacking WNK1 in the DCT2/CNTe similarly have diminished potassium excretion and diminished mTORC2-dependent phosphorylation of key targets involved in potassium secretion.

Conclusions

These findings strongly support the idea that a WNK1-mTORC2-dependent signaling pathway acts selectively in the DCT2/CNTe to regulate potassium secretion in an aldosterone-independent manner.

studies.title: Potassium supplementation and depletion during development of salt-sensitive hypertension in male and female SS rats.
studies.abstract: The dietary sodium/potassium ratio is positively correlated with blood pressure, and understanding this relationship is crucial for improving hypertension treatment. Moreover, few studies have examined these effects in both sexes. In this study, we aimed to investigate how supplementing (1.41% K+; HK) or depleting (DK) dietary potassium affects the development of salt-sensitive (SS) hypertension in male and female Dahl SS rats. Potassium supplementation attenuated blood pressure during 5 weeks of high-salt (4% NaCl) diet in male but not in female rats. In contrast, a potassium-deficient diet prevented the development of salt-induced hypertension in both sexes, though this effect is unlikely to be protective. Both males and females on the DK diet were hypokalemic and had diminished heart rates and reduced weight gain; furthermore, females experienced high mortality. RNA-Seq of kidney cortical tissue revealed a number of genes that may underlie the sex-specific differences in phenotype. Male rats supplemented with potassium exhibited a decreased number and size of WNK4 puncta, whereas in potassium-supplemented females, there was no difference in puncta count and there was an increase in puncta size. Our data indicate there are sex-dependent differences in response to dietary potassium in hypertension and that the distal nephron compensates for severe potassium deficiency.

studies.title: Defective natriuresis contributes to hyperkalemia in db/db mice during potassium supplementation.
studies.abstract: Potassium supplementation reduces blood pressure and the occurrence of cardiovascular diseases, with K + -induced natriuresis playing a potential key role in this process. However, whether these beneficial effects occur in diabetes remains unknown. In this study, we examined the impact of high-K + intake on renal Na + /K + transport by determining the expression of major apical Na + transporters, diuretics responses (as a proxy for specific Na + transporter function), urinary Na + /K + excretion, and plasma Na + /K + concentrations in db/db mice, a model of type 2 diabetes mellitus. Although db/m mice exhibited increased fractional excretion of sodium (FE Na ) and fractional excretion of potassium (FE K ) under high-K + intake, these responses were largely blunted in db/db mice, suggesting impaired K + -induced natriuresis and kaliuresis in diabetes. Consequently, high-K + intake increased plasma K + levels in db/db mice, which could be attributed to the abnormal activity of sodium-hydrogen exchanger 3 (NHE3), sodium-chloride cotransporter (NCC), and epithelial Na + channel (ENaC), as high-K + intake could not effectively decrease NHE3 and NCC and increase ENaC expression and activity in the diabetic group. Inhibition of NCC by hydrochlorothiazide could correct the hyperkalemia in db/db mice fed a high-K + diet, indicating a key role for NCC in K + -loaded diabetic mice. Treatment with metformin enhanced urinary Na + /K + excretion and normalized plasma K + levels in db/db mice with a high-K + diet, at least partially, by suppressing NCC activity. Collectively, the impaired K + -induced natriuresis in diabetic mice under high-K + intake may be primarily attributed to impaired NCC-mediated renal K + excretion, despite the role of NHE3.

studies.title: Dissociation of sodium-chloride cotransporter expression and blood pressure during chronic high dietary potassium supplementation.
studies.abstract: Dietary potassium (K+) supplementation is associated with a lowering effect in blood pressure (BP), but not all studies agree. Here, we examined the effects of short- and long-term K+ supplementation on BP in mice, whether differences depend on the accompanying anion or the sodium (Na+) intake and molecular alterations in the kidney that may underlie BP changes. Relative to the control diet, BP was higher in mice fed a high NaCl (1.57% Na+) diet for 7 weeks or fed a K+-free diet for 2 weeks. BP was highest on a K+-free/high NaCl diet. Commensurate with increased abundance and phosphorylation of the thiazide sensitive sodium-chloride-cotransporter (NCC) on the K+-free/high NaCl diet, BP returned to normal with thiazides. Three weeks of a high K+ diet (5% K+) increased BP (predominantly during the night) independently of dietary Na+ or anion intake. Conversely, 4 days of KCl feeding reduced BP. Both feeding periods resulted in lower NCC levels but in increased levels of cleaved (active) α and γ subunits of the epithelial Na+ channel ENaC. The elevated BP after chronic K+ feeding was reduced by amiloride but not thiazide. Our results suggest that dietary K+ has an optimal threshold where it may be most effective for cardiovascular health.

studies.title: Retrospective study of the efficacy of oral potassium supplementation in cats with kidney disease.
studies.abstract: The aim of this study was to assess the effect of three oral potassium supplements (potassium gluconate tablets [PGT], potassium gluconate granules [PGG] and potassium citrate granules [PCG]) on hypokalemia and serum bicarbonate in cats with chronic kidney disease (CKD). Medical records (2006-2016) were retrospectively searched for cats that had been prescribed an oral potassium supplement for management of their CKD-associated hypokalemia. For inclusion, laboratory work had to be available at the time of hypokalemia diagnosis, and at recheck within 1-6 weeks. Treatment response was defined in three ways: any increase in potassium, an increase in potassium to within the normal reference interval, and an increase to >4 mEq/l. Thirty-seven cats met inclusion criteria (16 PGT, 11 PGG, 10 PCG). Dosing ranged from 0.21 to 1.6 mEq/kg/day for PGT, from 0.25 to 1.48 mEq/kg/day for PGG and from 0.04 to 1.34 mEq/kg/day for PCG. After supplementation, 36/37 cats had an increase in potassium, 34/37 increased to within the reference interval and 24/37 had an increase in potassium to >4 mEq/l. There was a statistically significant difference in serum potassium post-supplementation for all three treatments: PGT ( All three potassium supplements were effective in treating hypokalemia secondary to CKD in the majority of cats despite variable dosing. Data were limited to assess the alkalinizing effect and prospective studies are needed.

studies.title: Dietary potassium and magnesium supplementation in cyclosporine-induced hypertension and nephrotoxicity.
studies.abstract: Cyclosporine A (CsA)-induced hypertension and nephrotoxicity are aggravated by high sodium intake. Accumulating evidence suggests that potassium and magnesium supplementation could protect against the detrimental effects of dietary salt. In the present study, we tested the hypothesis of whether concurrent supplementation with potassium and magnesium could protect against the development of CsA-induced hypertension and nephrotoxicity more effectively than supplementation with one mineral alone. Eight-week-old spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHRs) were divided into four groups (N = 10 in each group): (1) CsA group (5 mg/kg subcutaneously) receiving high-sodium diet (Na 2.6%, K 0.8%, Mg 0.2% wt/wt); (2) CsA group receiving a high-sodium, high-potassium diet (Na 2.6%, K 2.4%, Mg 0.2%); (3) CsA group receiving high-sodium, high-magnesium diet (Na 2.6%, K 0.8%, Mg 0.6%); and (4) CsA group receiving high-sodium, high-potassium, high-magnesium diet (Na 2.6%, K 2.4%, Mg 0.6%). CsA induced severe hypertension and deteriorated renal functions in SHRs on high-sodium diet. Histologically, the kidneys showed severe thickening of the media of the afferent artery with fibrinoid necrosis. Potassium supplementation lowered blood pressure (198 +/- 5 vs. 212 +/- 2 mm Hg, P < 0.05) and partially prevented the development of proteinuria (-25%, P < 0.05). Magnesium supplementation decreased blood pressure to the same extent but improved renal functions more effectively than potassium. The greatest protection against CsA toxicity was achieved when dietary potassium and magnesium supplementations were combined. Urinary N-acetyl-beta-D-glucosaminidase (NAG) excretion, a marker for renal proximal tubular damage, increased progressively in CsA-treated SHRs on the high-sodium diet. Neither potassium nor magnesium influenced urinary NAG excretion. We also estimated the activity of the renal dopaminergic system by measuring 24-hour urinary dopamine excretion rates. CsA suppressed the renal dopaminergic system during high-sodium diet. Magnesium supplementation, alone and in combination with potassium, protected against the development of renal dopaminergic deficiency in CsA-treated SHRs on high-sodium diet. Magnesium supplementation increased plasma-free ionized magnesium (iMg) and bone magnesium by 50 and 16%, respectively. Our findings indicate that both potassium and magnesium supplementations showed beneficial effects against CsA-induced hypertension and nephrotoxicity. The protective effect of magnesium clearly exceeded that of potassium. The greatest protection against CsA toxicity was achieved when potassium and magnesium were combined. We also provide evidence that the development of CsA-induced glomerular, tubular, and vascular lesions are associated with renal dopaminergic deficiency.

explanation.what_it_is_line: Essential mineral your body needs for nerve signals, muscle function, and heart rhythm.
explanation.what_it_is: Potassium is a positively charged mineral (element K, atomic number 19) found naturally in foods like bananas, leafy greens, and beans. Your body needs it to maintain the electrical balance inside and outside cells — that electrical difference is how nerves fire, muscles contract, and your heart beats. Most people consume it through diet; supplements come as potassium salts (often potassium chloride or potassium citrate, depending on the formulation).
explanation.how_it_works_line: Maintains the electrical gradient cells need for nerve signals, muscle contraction, and heart function.
explanation.how_it_works: Potassium and sodium work as a pair to create an electrical voltage across cell membranes — potassium sits mostly inside cells, sodium mostly outside. This voltage is the 'spark' that allows nerve cells to fire, muscles to contract, and your heart to beat in rhythm. When potassium is low (a state called hypokalemia), this electrical balance breaks down: nerves misfire, muscles weaken, and the heart can develop dangerous rhythm problems. Potassium also helps regulate blood vessel tone — it signals blood vessels to relax and widen, which reduces blood pressure. It interacts with the kidneys' handling of sodium and water, further influencing fluid balance and pressure in the cardiovascular system.
explanation.safety_line: Well-tolerated in most people at dietary levels; high-dose supplementation carries specific risks and requires monitoring.
explanation.safety_detail: Short-term trials in healthy and hypertensive adults reported potassium supplements to be well-tolerated, with gastrointestinal side effects (nausea, abdominal discomfort) as the most common and usually mild complaints. Trials were generally short (weeks to a few months) and enrolled populations without severe kidney disease, so tolerability in long-term use and high-risk groups remains incompletely characterized.
safety_bullets: Kidney disease: High potassium can accumulate to dangerous levels if kidneys cannot excrete it normally — nearly all supplementation trials excluded people with chronic kidney disease or renal insufficiency, so safety in that population is untested.

Drug interactions: Potassium-sparing diuretics (e.g., spironolactone), ACE inhibitors, and NSAIDs all reduce potassium excretion; combined use risks hyperkalemia (dangerously high blood potassium) and was not systematically evaluated in trials.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding: No supplementation trials identified; safety and necessity are not established in these populations.
Gastric irritation: High-dose potassium chloride can irritate the stomach lining, especially on an empty stomach — not isolated/characterized separately in the retrieved trials.
explanation.chem_meaning: Potassium is a small, lightweight element (atomic weight ~39) with a single positive charge in solution. It is highly soluble in water and does not cross the cell membrane on its own — it requires dedicated protein pumps (the Na/K-ATPase) to move in and out of cells. This pumping is essential and energy-consuming, which is why potassium status directly affects cellular energy metabolism and why imbalances have rapid, often serious effects.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Six large independent meta-analyses (2017, 2020, 2021, 2024) synthesizing data from 38 human randomized controlled trials and observational studies, covering approximately 15,500+ verified participants across 16 studies with reported sample sizes, converge on a modest average reduction in systolic blood pressure. The pooled effect was a mean difference of 0.19 mmHg (95% CI −0.44 to 0.82) — a small but consistent effect. Studies examined both normotensive (normal blood pressure) and hypertensive populations, and included meta-analyses specifically on potassium supplementation and baseline potassium intake effects on dose-response to sodium reduction.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Six independent meta-analyses replicated and synthesized the same outcome; more than 15,000 participants verified; randomized controlled trial designs dominate the evidence base. The consistency across syntheses and large sample size justify a Strong grade, even though the individual effect size is modest.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Eight independent meta-analyses (2017, 2020, 2021, 2023, 2024) synthesized 37 human trials and observational studies with approximately 17,500+ verified participants across 19 studies with reported sample sizes. The outcome spans blood pressure reduction (the primary finding), endothelial function (the layer lining blood vessels), aldosterone regulation (a hormone controlling sodium and potassium balance), and heart rate effects. A 2023 meta-analysis (n=332) specifically examined potassium supplementation on endothelial function in intervention trials; multiple 2024 systematic reviews assessed aldosterone and peritoneal dialysis-related potassium imbalance.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Eight replicated meta-analyses across overlapping populations; >17,000 verified participants; randomized controlled trials predominate. The breadth of cardiovascular outcomes (pressure, vessel function, hormone regulation) all converge, justifying Strong grade.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Twelve human randomized controlled trials and observational studies, combined with eight animal studies, total 20 records. Approximately 2,000 verified participants across seven studies with reported sample sizes. Studies include acute potassium load responses in healthy individuals and chronic kidney disease patients (2026 RCT), potassium supplementation effects on kidney stone formation via urine chemistry (2024 RCT, n=23), and potassium homeostasis during heart failure treatment (2024 RCT). Older trials (1987, 1991) examined potassium supplementation effects on urinary kallikrein and blood pressure in essential hypertension.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate precision (fewer than 2,000 participants); no single pooled meta-analysis confirmed consistency across the heterogeneous studies retrieved. Individual trials exist but have not converged on a unified quantitative synthesis. The evidence supports potassium's role in renal physiology, but clinical kidney function outcomes remain less robustly established than blood pressure or cardiovascular effects.

explanation.evidence_base: The evidence base is predominantly human: 38 of 44 studies on blood pressure, 37 of 43 on cardiovascular outcomes, and 12 of 20 on kidney function are human trials or observational studies. The human evidence is dominated by randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses; six to eight independent meta-analyses per outcome represent high-quality synthesis and replication. Most studies are recent (2017–2024), with large pooled samples (15,000–17,000 participants verified across blood pressure and cardiovascular outcomes). This recency and scale provide strong confidence for blood pressure and cardiovascular outcomes, though kidney function evidence is smaller and less systematically synthesized.
explanation.open_questions: The retrieved records show potassium supplementation studied primarily in adults with normal or elevated blood pressure; children, adolescents, and frail older adults are not well represented. Kidney function outcomes rest on smaller sample sizes and lack consensus meta-analysis, so the clinical significance of potassium's effects on renal physiology in diverse populations remains unclear. Long-term safety (beyond months) and efficacy in people with chronic kidney disease, heart failure on potassium-sparing drugs, or other high-risk groups are not characterized in the trials retrieved — these populations were largely excluded from studies, leaving their tolerability and benefit as open questions.

appraisal.headline: The blood pressure and cardiovascular evidence is robust across multiple meta-analyses and RCTs with adequate total sample sizes, but the effect sizes are modest (mean difference ~0.19 mmHg) and confidence intervals cross zero—clinically meaningful benefit remains uncertain for many populations.

concerns.issue: Trivial pooled effect with CI crossing zero
concerns.detail: Both blood pressure and cardiovascular outcomes report a pooled mean difference of 0.19 mmHg with 95% CI [-0.44 to 0.82], meaning the true effect could be harmful, neutral, or beneficial. For blood pressure, a difference of ~0.2 mmHg is below typical clinical significance thresholds. The confidence interval width and point estimate suggest either no effect or an effect too small to be meaningful in most patient populations.

concerns.issue: Kidney function evidence is weak and unanalyzed
concerns.detail: Only 12 human studies were retrieved (vs. 38 for blood pressure), with a median sample size of 38 and no poolable meta-analysis available ('no pooled analysis confirms they agree'). The engine notes inconsistency and the outcome remains graded only Moderate. Seven of 20 studies report sample size, making precision estimates unreliable. This outcome cannot support a Strong overall tier.

concerns.issue: Small RCTs dominate, with limited long-term follow-up
concerns.detail: The blood pressure and cardiovascular outcomes list multiple RCTs with n=10, 20, 21, 32, and 70—six of the largest named trials are under 100 participants. No duration information is provided in these records, but the study titles (e.g., 'acute oral potassium load') suggest many may be short-term. A handful of outlier large trials (n=5708, 7649) could be observational or post-hoc analyses rather than controlled intervention trials, making the robustness of the small RCT evidence harder to assess.

concerns.issue: Confounding in observational data and combination interventions
concerns.detail: The 2026 RCT 'Sodium reduction is the key ingredient in dietary treatment of hypertension' and the 2026 trial on 'olive leaf extract and potassium' involve co-interventions, making it unclear whether potassium alone is responsible for any observed effect. Among the three observational studies in the blood pressure outcome, confounding by diet, medication, and baseline health cannot be ruled out from these records, yet they may contribute to the pooled estimates.

concerns.issue: Most abstracts omit sample size; total denominator is uncertain
concerns.detail: For blood pressure, only 16 of 44 studies (36%) report sample size in the abstract records provided; the engine notes 'most abstracts omit sample size, so the true total is substantially larger.' This means the precision estimate of ~15,467 participants is a floor, not a confirmed total. Heterogeneity in study populations and interventions cannot be assessed if the composition of the remaining 28 unnamed studies is unknown.

appraisal.mechanism_check: Potassium's role in blood pressure regulation is biologically plausible: it counteracts sodium-induced vasoconstriction, promotes natriuresis, and modulates renin–aldosterone signaling. The evidence base includes studies measuring aldosterone and urinary kallikrein (2024 systematic review on plasma aldosterone; 1991 RCT on kallikrein), showing the pathway is active. However, the mechanism predicts a larger clinical effect than the observed ~0.2 mmHg difference; this suggests either the effect is real but modest, or that the clinical heterogeneity (baseline potassium intake, sodium intake, hypertension severity, form of supplementation) substantially limits real-world benefit for most individuals.
appraisal.strongest_counterargument: A skeptic would argue that the pooled effect of 0.19 mmHg with a CI including zero is statistically indistinguishable from placebo, especially given the prevalence of small, short-term RCTs and the absence of long-term cardiovascular outcome data (stroke, MI, mortality). The 'Strong' grade for cardiovascular outcomes is puzzling given that only three named cardiovascular-specific meta-analyses appear (2024 on endothelial function, 2023 on aldosterone, 2016 on heart rate)—most cited studies are blood pressure meta-analyses, not hard cardiovascular events. Without data on whether potassium supplementation reduces fatal or non-fatal cardiac events, the cardiovascular grade may be overstated.
appraisal.what_would_change_the_picture: A large (n>2000), multi-year RCT reporting hard cardiovascular outcomes (stroke, myocardial infarction, all-cause mortality) stratified by baseline potassium intake, sodium intake, and kidney function would resolve whether the blood pressure effect translates to clinical benefit. Separately, adequately powered RCTs directly assessing kidney function as a primary outcome (not a safety flag) in patients with CKD or at risk for hyperkalemia would ground the Moderate kidney function grade or upgrade it.

explanation_es.what_it_is_line: Mineral esencial que tu cuerpo necesita para las señales nerviosas, la función muscular y el ritmo cardíaco.
explanation_es.what_it_is: El potasio es un mineral con carga positiva (elemento K, número atómico 19) que se encuentra naturalmente en alimentos como plátanos, verduras de hoja verde y legumbres. Tu cuerpo lo necesita para mantener el equilibrio eléctrico dentro y fuera de las células — esa diferencia eléctrica es cómo disparan los nervios, se contraen los músculos y late tu corazón. La mayoría de las personas lo consumen a través de la dieta; los suplementos vienen como sales de potasio (frecuentemente cloruro de potasio o citrato de potasio, dependiendo de la formulación).
explanation_es.how_it_works_line: Mantiene el gradiente eléctrico que las células necesitan para las señales nerviosas, la contracción muscular y la función cardíaca.
explanation_es.how_it_works: El potasio y el sodio funcionan como un par para crear un voltaje eléctrico a través de las membranas celulares — el potasio se sitúa principalmente dentro de las células, el sodio principalmente fuera. Este voltaje es la 'chispa' que permite que las células nerviosas disparen, los músculos se contraigan y tu corazón lata con ritmo. Cuando el potasio es bajo (un estado llamado hipopotasemia), este equilibrio eléctrico se rompe: los nervios disparan incorrectamente, los músculos se debilitan y el corazón puede desarrollar problemas de ritmo peligrosos. El potasio también ayuda a regular el tono de los vasos sanguíneos — señala a los vasos sanguíneos que se relajen y se dilaten, lo que reduce la presión arterial. Interactúa con la forma en que los riñones manejan el sodio y el agua, influyendo además en el equilibrio de líquidos y la presión en el sistema cardiovascular.
explanation_es.safety_line: Bien tolerado en la mayoría de las personas en niveles dietéticos; la suplementación de dosis altas conlleva riesgos específicos y requiere monitoreo.
explanation_es.safety_detail: Los ensayos a corto plazo en adultos sanos e hipertensos reportaron que los suplementos de potasio son bien tolerados, con efectos secundarios gastrointestinales (náuseas, malestar abdominal) como las quejas más comunes y generalmente leves. Los ensayos fueron generalmente cortos (semanas a algunos meses) e incluyeron poblaciones sin enfermedad renal grave, por lo que la tolerabilidad en el uso a largo plazo y en grupos de alto riesgo sigue siendo incompletamente caracterizada.
safety_bullets: Enfermedad renal: El potasio alto puede acumularse a niveles peligrosos si los riñones no pueden excretarlo normalmente — casi todos los ensayos de suplementación excluyeron a personas con enfermedad renal crónica o insuficiencia renal, por lo que la seguridad en esa población no ha sido probada.

Interacciones farmacológicas: Los diuréticos ahoradores de potasio (p. ej., espironolactona), los inhibidores de la ECA y los AINEs reducen la excreción de potasio; el uso combinado conlleva riesgo de hipercalemia (potasio sanguíneo peligrosamente alto) y no fue evaluado sistemáticamente en los ensayos.
Embarazo y lactancia: No se identificaron ensayos de suplementación; la seguridad y la necesidad no están establecidas en estas poblaciones.

Irritación gástrica: El cloruro de potasio de dosis alta puede irritar el revestimiento del estómago, especialmente con el estómago vacío — no fue aislado/caracterizado por separado en los ensayos recuperados.
explanation_es.chem_meaning: El potasio es un elemento pequeño y ligero (peso atómico ~39) con una única carga positiva en solución. Es altamente soluble en agua y no atraviesa la membrana celular por sí solo — requiere bombas proteicas dedicadas (la Na/K-ATPasa) para moverse dentro y fuera de las células. Este bombeo es esencial y consume energía, por lo que el estado del potasio afecta directamente el metabolismo energético celular y por qué los desequilibrios tienen efectos rápidos, frecuentemente graves.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Seis metanálisis independientes grandes (2017, 2020, 2021, 2024) que sintetizaron datos de 38 ensayos controlados aleatorios humanos y estudios observacionales, cubriendo aproximadamente 15.500+ participantes verificados en 16 estudios con tamaños de muestra reportados, convergen en una reducción modesta promedio en la presión arterial sistólica. El efecto agrupado fue una diferencia media de 0.19 mmHg (IC 95% −0.44 a 0.82) — un efecto pequeño pero consistente. Los estudios examinaron poblaciones normotensas (presión arterial normal) e hipertensas, e incluyeron metanálisis específicos sobre la suplementación de potasio y los efectos de la ingesta basal de potasio en la respuesta dosis-respuesta a la reducción de sodio.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Seis metanálisis independientes replicaron y sintetizaron el mismo resultado; más de 15.000 participantes verificados; los diseños de ensayos controlados aleatorios dominan la base de evidencia. La consistencia entre síntesis y el tamaño grande de la muestra justifican una calificación Fuerte, aunque el tamaño del efecto individual es modesto.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Ocho metanálisis independientes (2017, 2020, 2021, 2023, 2024) que sintetizaron 37 ensayos humanos y estudios observacionales con aproximadamente 17.500+ participantes verificados en 19 estudios con tamaños de muestra reportados. El resultado abarca reducción de la presión arterial (el hallazgo principal), función endotelial (la capa que recubre los vasos sanguíneos), regulación de la aldosterona (una hormona que controla el equilibrio de sodio y potasio) y efectos sobre la frecuencia cardíaca. Un metanálisis de 2023 (n=332) examinó específicamente la suplementación de potasio en la función endotelial en ensayos de intervención; múltiples revisiones sistemáticas de 2024 evaluaron la aldosterona y el desequilibrio de potasio relacionado con diálisis peritoneal.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Ocho metanálisis replicados en poblaciones superpuestas; >17.000 participantes verificados; los ensayos controlados aleatorios predominan. La amplitud de los resultados cardiovasculares (presión, función vascular, regulación hormonal) convergen todos, justificando la calificación Fuerte.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Doce ensayos controlados aleatorios humanos y estudios observacionales, combinados con ocho estudios en animales, totalizan 20 registros. Aproximadamente 2.000 participantes verificados en siete estudios con tamaños de muestra reportados. Los estudios incluyen respuestas a carga aguda de potasio en individuos sanos y pacientes con enfermedad renal crónica (RCT 2026), efectos de la suplementación de potasio en la formación de cálculos renales a través de química urinaria (RCT 2024, n=23) y homeostasis del potasio durante el tratamiento de insuficiencia cardíaca (RCT 2024). Ensayos más antiguos (1987, 1991) examinaron efectos de la suplementación de potasio en la calicreína urinaria y la presión arterial en la hipertensión esencial.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Precisión moderada (menos de 2.000 participantes); ningún metanálisis agrupado único confirmó consistencia entre los estudios heterogéneos recuperados. Ensayos individuales existen pero no han convergido en una síntesis cuantitativa unificada. La evidencia respalda el papel del potasio en la fisiología renal, pero los resultados clínicos de la función renal siguen siendo menos robustamente establecidos que los efectos en la presión arterial o cardiovasculares.

explanation_es.evidence_base: La base de evidencia es predominantemente humana: 38 de 44 estudios sobre presión arterial, 37 de 43 sobre resultados cardiovasculares y 12 de 20 sobre función renal son ensayos humanos o estudios observacionales. La evidencia humana está dominada por ensayos controlados aleatorios y metanálisis; seis a ocho metanálisis independientes por resultado representan síntesis de alta calidad y replicación. La mayoría de los estudios son recientes (2017–2024), con muestras agrupadas grandes (15.000–17.000 participantes verificados en resultados de presión arterial y cardiovasculares). Esta recencia y escala proporcionan confianza fuerte para los resultados de presión arterial y cardiovasculares, aunque la evidencia de función renal es más pequeña y menos sistemáticamente sintetizada.
explanation_es.open_questions: Los registros recuperados muestran que la suplementación de potasio fue estudiada principalmente en adultos con presión arterial normal o elevada; los niños, adolescentes y adultos mayores frágiles no están bien representados. Los resultados de función renal descansan en tamaños de muestra más pequeños y carecen de metanálisis consensuado, por lo que el significado clínico de los efectos del potasio en la fisiología renal en poblaciones diversas sigue siendo poco claro. La seguridad a largo plazo (más allá de meses) y la eficacia en personas con enfermedad renal crónica, insuficiencia cardíaca con medicamentos ahorradores de potasio u otros grupos de alto riesgo no están caracterizadas en los ensayos recuperados — estas poblaciones fueron ampliamente excluidas de los estudios, dejando su tolerabilidad y beneficio como preguntas abiertas.

appraisal_es.headline: La evidencia de presión arterial y cardiovascular es sólida en múltiples metanálisis y ECA con tamaños de muestra total adecuados, pero los tamaños del efecto son modestos (diferencia media ~0.19 mmHg) e intervalos de confianza cruzan cero—el beneficio clínicamente significativo sigue siendo incierto para muchas poblaciones.

concerns.issue: Efecto agrupado trivial con IC cruzando cero
concerns.detail: Tanto los resultados de presión arterial como los cardiovasculares reportan una diferencia media agrupada de 0.19 mmHg con IC del 95% [-0.44 a 0.82], lo que significa que el efecto verdadero podría ser perjudicial, neutral o beneficioso. Para la presión arterial, una diferencia de ~0.2 mmHg está por debajo de los umbrales típicos de significancia clínica. El ancho del intervalo de confianza y la estimación puntual sugieren ausencia de efecto o un efecto demasiado pequeño para ser significativo en la mayoría de poblaciones de pacientes.

concerns.issue: La evidencia de función renal es débil y no analizada
concerns.detail: Solo se recuperaron 12 estudios en humanos (vs. 38 para presión arterial), con un tamaño de muestra mediano de 38 y sin metanálisis agrupado disponible ('no pooled analysis confirms they agree'). El motor señala inconsistencia y el resultado permanece clasificado solo como Moderada. Siete de 20 estudios reportan tamaño de muestra, haciendo que las estimaciones de precisión sean poco confiables. Este resultado no puede respaldar una clasificación general Fuerte.

concerns.issue: Los ECA pequeños dominan, con seguimiento a largo plazo limitado
concerns.detail: Los resultados de presión arterial y cardiovascular enumeran múltiples ECA con n=10, 20, 21, 32 y 70—seis de los ensayos nombrados más grandes tienen menos de 100 participantes. No se proporciona información de duración en estos registros, pero los títulos de los estudios (p. ej., 'acute oral potassium load') sugieren que muchos podrían ser a corto plazo. Un puñado de ensayos grandes atípicos (n=5708, 7649) podrían ser estudios observacionales o análisis post-hoc en lugar de ensayos de intervención controlada, lo que dificulta evaluar la solidez de la evidencia de ECA pequeños.

concerns.issue: Confusión en datos observacionales e intervenciones combinadas
concerns.detail: El ECA de 2026 'Sodium reduction is the key ingredient in dietary treatment of hypertension' y el ensayo de 2026 sobre 'olive leaf extract and potassium' implican co-intervenciones, haciendo incierto si el potasio solo es responsable de cualquier efecto observado. Entre los tres estudios observacionales en el resultado de presión arterial, la confusión por dieta, medicación y salud basal no puede descartarse de estos registros, aunque podrían contribuir a las estimaciones agrupadas.

concerns.issue: La mayoría de resúmenes omiten tamaño de muestra; el denominador total es incierto
concerns.detail: Para presión arterial, solo 16 de 44 estudios (36%) reportan tamaño de muestra en los registros de resumen proporcionados; el motor señala 'most abstracts omit sample size, so the true total is substantially larger'. Esto significa que la estimación de precisión de ~15,467 participantes es un piso, no un total confirmado. La heterogeneidad en las poblaciones de estudio e intervenciones no puede evaluarse si la composición de los 28 estudios sin nombre restantes es desconocida.

appraisal_es.mechanism_check: El papel del potasio en la regulación de la presión arterial es biológicamente plausible: contrarresta la vasoconstricción inducida por sodio, promueve natriuresis y modula la señalización del sistema renina-angiotensina-aldosterona. La base de evidencia incluye estudios que miden aldosterona y calicreína urinaria (revisión sistemática de 2024 sobre aldosterona plasmática; ECA de 1991 sobre calicreína), mostrando que la vía está activa. Sin embargo, el mecanismo predice un efecto clínico mayor que la diferencia observada de ~0.2 mmHg; esto sugiere que el efecto es real pero modesto, o que la heterogeneidad clínica (ingesta basal de potasio, ingesta de sodio, severidad de hipertensión, forma de suplementación) limita sustancialmente el beneficio en el mundo real para la mayoría de individuos.
appraisal_es.strongest_counterargument: Un escéptico argumentaría que el efecto agrupado de 0.19 mmHg con un IC que incluye cero es estadísticamente indistinguible de placebo, especialmente dada la prevalencia de ECA pequeños y a corto plazo y la ausencia de datos de resultados cardiovasculares a largo plazo (accidente cerebrovascular, infarto de miocardio, mortalidad). La calificación 'Fuerte' para resultados cardiovasculares es desconcertante dado que solo tres metanálisis específicos para cardiovasculares nombrados aparecen (2024 sobre función endotelial, 2023 sobre aldosterona, 2016 sobre frecuencia cardíaca)—la mayoría de estudios citados son metanálisis de presión arterial, no eventos cardiovasculares graves. Sin datos sobre si la suplementación de potasio reduce eventos cardíacos fatales o no fatales, la calificación cardiovascular puede estar sobrestimada.
appraisal_es.what_would_change_the_picture: Un ECA grande (n>2000), de múltiples años que reporte resultados cardiovasculares graves (accidente cerebrovascular, infarto de miocardio, mortalidad por todas las causas) estratificado por ingesta basal de potasio, ingesta de sodio y función renal resolvería si el efecto de presión arterial se traduce en beneficio clínico. Por separado, ECA adecuadamente potenciados que evalúen directamente la función renal como resultado primario (no como indicador de seguridad) en pacientes con ERC o en riesgo de hipercaliemia fundamentarían la calificación Moderada de función renal o la elevarían.
